chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Muhammad ibn Hafsh, from Mansur, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man has a sheep in his possession, then another man came and claimed it, and established the testimony of just witnesses that it was born with him, and he had not given it as a gift nor sold it. And the one who had it in his possession came with testimony like theirs, of just witnesses, that it was born with him, and he had not sold it nor given it as a gift.

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Its right belongs to the claimant, and I do not accept testimony from the one who has it in his possession, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, only commanded that the testimony be sought from the claimant. If he has testimony, [it is accepted]; otherwise, the oath of the one who is in possession [is taken]. Thus did Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, command.'
ai.seo_question: How does Shia jurisprudence resolve a dispute when both the claimant and the possessor provide equal testimony of ownership?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudential ruling when two parties present equal, valid testimonies (*bayyinatayn*) regarding ownership, establishing that the claimant prevails over the possessor. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) grounds this decision in the Quranic principle that the burden of proof (*bayyinah*) rests primarily on the claimant, while the possessor provides an oath (*yamin*) if the claimant's evidence is matched. This ruling highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on balancing evidentiary weight with the presumption of possession in civil disputes.
